title: Pullman's Other Son
premise: A German sergeant swore George Pullman was his father. He followed the family for four years, to the office, to the funeral, to the front steps, and once to the wrong end of a judge's gun.

opening.text:
JAUNT: PULLMAN'S OTHER SON. A Monday afternoon in November 1904, outside the Pullman house at Eighteenth Street.

Four stops, around the Pullman house and down the street to the house of the family's son-in-law. George Pullman had twin sons, and the whole city knew their names. There was a third young man who claimed the name too. His mother told him on her deathbed who his father was, and he crossed an ocean to say so to Pullman's face. The family called him a madman. The doctors kept saying he was sane.

Start at the front of the house, where his story begins.

stops.text: 1729 Prairie, the Pullman house. Picture a German Army sergeant named Gustave Behring, 28 years old, at his mother's bedside. Dying, she told him his real father was George M. Pullman. She had been a governess in Chicago "for a house on the west side", she said, and when she became pregnant, Pullman packed her off to Germany with $500. Behring came to Chicago. He went to the Pullman building and was thrown out of Pullman's office. He was locked up for a time in an asylum, and arrested six more times lurking outside the building. Four days before Pullman died, their conversation was recorded. "BEHRING: You are my father! PULLMAN: You are a crazy man!" The house will be razed in 1922. Walk round to the front steps.

stage.caption: A stranger in a dark coat stops on the walk at the Pullman gate, looks up at the house, and walks on.

cast.name: A stranger at the gate (unnamed; nobody is known to have been here on this day)

stops.text: The front steps. Pullman died in October 1897. His family buried him under concrete and steel. And "Less than 12 hours after the funeral, Behring showed up at the family's residence on Prairie Avenue, demanding to speak to Mrs. Harriett Pullman." He never reached the door. On these steps he was met by Pullman's two sons, the twins, and by the family's lawyers. He was arrested again, and on 29 October 1897 an insanity expert examined him and pronounced him sane. Not a madman, then. Just a man who would not go away. The Pullmans' housekeeper, Emma Scott, still answers this door. Walk round the corner to the glasshouse.

stage.caption: Emma Scott, the housekeeper, opens the front door, looks out at the empty steps, and closes it again.

stops.text: The conservatory, the family's glass parlour. Behind this glass the Pullmans waited for the problem to leave. In September 1898 it did: detectives walked Behring up the gangway of the Cunard liner Campania, bound for Bremen. Europe could have him. But he came back. A man who has been told by his dying mother who his father was does not stay deported. And by 1901 the twins who had blocked the steps had troubles of their own. One of them, George Jr., would be dead by November. Florence Pullman's husband, Frank Lowden, was a lawyer. So when Behring came back, he went to Lowden. Walk south down Prairie to the Lowden house.

stage.caption: The groom Samuel Whatter Jr. comes out of the stable yard by the glasshouse and stands looking down the street.

stops.text: 1912 Prairie, where Frank Lowden lives with Florence and their children. Lowden is a careful man, but even careful men have bad afternoons. "on June 25, 1901, Behring was again arrested at the law offices of Frank Lowden (Florence Pullman's husband) demanding $5,000 in cash and $10,000 a month for 6 months." Lowden's partner did not wait for the police to talk him out of it: "Judge Davis, Lowden's partner, held Behring at gunpoint until the police arrived". The house will be razed in 1939. Watch Lowden come home this afternoon, and look back down the street before he goes in.

stage.caption: Frank Lowden comes up his walk, stops on the steps to look back down the street, and goes in.

legs.story: Round to the front steps, where the twins and the lawyers met him after the funeral.
Along the side of the house to the conservatory.
South down Prairie Avenue to 1912, the house of the family's lawyer.

endings.text: End of the walk. Gustave Behring was arrested, locked up, examined, found sane, put on a ship and arrested again, and as the papers told it his story ends at the point of a judge's gun. "You are my father!" "You are a crazy man!" Those two sentences are all that is left of the only conversation the two men ever had, and you can decide for yourself which of them was telling the truth.

keepsake.title: A Claim on the Pullman Name
keepsake.text: An interpretive card of the Behring affair of 1897 to 1901 as the papers reported it, not a historical artifact.

evidence.text: Gustave Behring, 28, a sergeant in the German Army, was told on his mother's deathbed that his real father was George M. Pullman. She said she had been a governess in Chicago 'for a house on the west side'; when she became pregnant Pullman allegedly packed her off to Germany and supplied her with $500.
evidence.locator: The page's second paragraph, after the Cedar Rapids Evening Gazette, 14 December 1897.

evidence.text: At the Pullman building Pullman threw him out of his office; Behring was confined for a time in a mental institution, and was arrested six times more lurking outside the building. Four days before Pullman's death the conversation was recorded: BEHRING: You are my father! PULLMAN: You are a crazy man!
George M. Pullman Residence, 1729 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1922.

Pullman's Other Son: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

Pullman's Other Son: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

'Less than 12 hours after the funeral, Behring showed up at the family's residence on Prairie Avenue, demanding to speak to Mrs. Harriett Pullman.' He was met on the steps by Pullman's sons and the family lawyers, and was eventually arrested again; on 29 October 1897 an insanity expert pronounced him sane.

Fearing his body would be dug up, the family had him buried in a 'lead-lined mahogany coffin, which was then sealed inside a block of concrete', under steel rails 'bolted together at right angles', at Graceland Cemetery. An 1897 New York Times account gives a 'lead-lined box wrapped in tar paper' and 'an inch of asphaltum'; behind it, 'a lot of high-profile grave robberies lately' and the fear that 'some of the employees weren't quite done getting revenge'. The historian Adam Selzer: 'Whether it's true or not, we don't really know.'
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraph on the burial; the WTTW piece on the grave.

evidence.text: In 1894 Pullman cut his workers' wages, but 'he didn't reduce the rent in Pullman', his company town; he 'died of a heart attack' on 19 October 1897.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on the strike and his death.

evidence.text: In September 1898 detectives escorted Behring to the Cunard liner Campania, bound for Bremen.
evidence.locator: The page's sixth paragraph, after the New York Times.

evidence.text: George, Jr. secretly married Lynn Fernald, 'his brother's betrothed'. Frederick Bowers sued George for $100,000, 'eventually settling for $50,000.' George died of complications from pneumonia in November, 1901.
evidence.locator: The page's fourth, sixth and eighth paragraphs.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book lists Mr. and Mrs. Frank Orren Lowden at 1912 Prairie; Florence Pullman married Frank Lowden.
evidence.locator: Blue Book, Prairie Av. street list, '1912 Mr. & Mrs. Frank Orren Lowden'; the children page.

evidence.text: 'on June 25, 1901, Behring was again arrested at the law offices of Frank Lowden (Florence Pullman's husband) demanding $5,000 in cash and $10,000 a month for 6 months. Judge Davis, Lowden's partner, held Behring at gunpoint until the police arrived'.
Bryan P. Moulton Residence, 1912 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1939.
